claims.source: The cells proliferated ~10,000 fold and the enucleation rate was >90% in both the CD55-null cells and wild-type controls, demonstrating that the progenitors differentiated efficiently and that CD55 is not required for this process (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that CD55-null cells differentiated as efficiently as wild-type controls.

claims.claim: Invasion into CD55-CRISPR cRBCs on day 18 was reduced by ~40% compared to control cells.
claims.source: While invasion into the CD55-CRISPR cRBCs was impaired relative to the control cells, it was only reduced by ~40% (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Approximately 50% of the enucleated cRBCs on day 17 were CD71-positive and ~50% were CD71 negative.
claims.source: Flow cytometry on day 17 demonstrated that approximately 50% of the enucleated cRBCs were CD71-positive and ~50% were CD71 negative, indicating a mix of cell maturity in the population (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Day 17 cRBCs were ~50% reticulocytes and 50% erythrocytes.
claims.source: This was further validated using a reticulocyte stain (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), which showed that day 17 cells were ~50% reticulocytes and 50% erythrocytes.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Invasion assays with P. falciparum strain 3D7 using CD71-negative cRBCs showed a ~75% reduction in invasion into the CD55-CRISPR cRBCs as compared to isogenic control cRBCs.
claims.source: Using these highly mature cells, invasion assays with P. falciparum strain 3D7 showed a ~75% reduction in invasion into the CD55-CRISPR cRBCs as compared to isogenic control cRBCs in three biological replicate experiments (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: P. falciparum invasion was restricted to the cells expressing CD55 in the CD55-CRISPR population.
claims.source: This was confirmed by immunofluorescence assays showing that P. falciparum invasion was restricted to the cells expressing CD55: the parasitemia in the minority, CD55-positive cells in the population was 22.5%, whereas less than 0.5% of the CD55-null cRBCs were infected (Figure 1F–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F–G.

claims.claim: CD55 is critical for P. falciparum invasion of fully differentiated cRBCs.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that CD55 is critical for P. falciparum invasion of fully differentiated cRBCs, mimicking the prior observations with natural CD55-null erythrocytes, and validating CD55 as an essential host factor for P. falciparum invasion.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing reduced invasion in CD55-null cRBCs.

claims.claim: High levels of other receptors important for invasion, such as basigin, may explain the reduced requirement for CD55 for P. falciparum invasion of younger, CD71-positive reticulocytes.
claims.source: Based on previous observations that the expression levels of many RBC surface proteins decline during reticulocyte maturation (Chu et al., 2018; Malleret et al., 2013), we hypothesize that high levels of other receptors important for invasion, such as basigin, may explain the reduced requirement for CD55 for P. falciparum invasion of younger, CD71-positive reticulocytes.
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on prior observations about protein expression during reticulocyte maturation.

claims.claim: None of the anti-CD55 monoclonal antibodies individually affected parasite growth.
claims.source: While none of the antibodies individually affected parasite growth, we observed a dose-dependent inhibition of parasite growth over 72 hr in the presence of all three anti-CD55 monoclonal antibodies combined, in comparison to an isotype control (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: A dose-dependent inhibition of parasite growth over 72 hr was observed in the presence of all three anti-CD55 monoclonal antibodies combined.
claims.source: While none of the antibodies individually affected parasite growth, we observed a dose-dependent inhibition of parasite growth over 72 hr in the presence of all three anti-CD55 monoclonal antibodies combined, in comparison to an isotype control (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: At the highest antibody concentration tested (500 µg/ml), the relative parasitemia was reduced by ~40% in the presence of the combined monoclonals, compared to the isotype control.
claims.source: At the highest antibody concentration tested (500 µg/ml), the relative parasitemia was reduced by ~40% in the presence of the combined monoclonals, compared to the isotype control.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from the antibody inhibition experiments.

claims.claim: A dose-dependent inhibition of parasite growth was observed in the presence of anti-CD55 polyclonal antibody relative to isotype control, with a ~40% reduction in relative parasitemia at the highest concentration of antibody (400 µg/ml).
claims.source: In P. falciparum growth assays, we observed a dose-dependent inhibition of parasite growth in the presence of anti-CD55 antibody relative to isotype control, with a ~ 40% reduction in relative parasitemia at the highest concentration of antibody (400 µg/ml) (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The growth of P. falciparum strain 3D7 was inhibited ~40% in NM-treated RBCs as compared to untreated cells in the absence of antibody.
claims.source: As has been described previously, the growth of P. falciparum strain 3D7 was inhibited ~40% in NM-treated RBCs as compared to untreated cells in the absence of antibody (Figure 2C), reflecting some reliance of strain 3D7 on sialic acid for efficient invasion.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: A dose-dependent inhibition of parasite growth was observed in NM-treated cells in the presence of increasing concentrations of anti-CD55 antibody that is similar to untreated cells (~60% versus~40% at maximum concentration of antibody).
claims.source: In the presence of increasing concentrations of anti-CD55 antibody, we observed a dose-dependent inhibition of parasite growth in the NM-treated cells that is similar to untreated cells (~60% versus~40% at maximum concentration of antibody) (Figure 2B–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B–C.

claims.claim: CD55 blockade inhibits P. falciparum regardless of the presence of membrane sialic acid.
claims.source: The finding that CD55 blockade inhibits P. falciparum regardless of the presence of membrane sialic acid suggests that CD55 plays a role in both sialic-acid-dependent and -independent invasion.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that anti-CD55 antibody inhibits invasion in both NM-treated and untreated cells.

claims.claim: In the presence of 400 µg/ml of anti-CD55 Fab fragments, a ~40% reduction in relative parasitemia was observed.
claims.source: In the presence of 400 µg/ml of anti-CD55 Fab fragments, we observed ~40% reduction in relative parasitemia, recapitulating the growth inhibitory activity observed with the bivalent anti-CD55 IgG antibody (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: In the presence of the isotype control antibody, 53 out of 345 P. falciparum merozoites that contacted an RBC invaded successfully (15%).
claims.source: In the presence of the isotype control antibody, of 345 P. falciparum merozoites that contacted an RBC, 53 invaded successfully (15%) (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Out of 312 merozoites that made contact with an RBC in the presence of anti-CD55, only 21 successfully invaded (6.7%).
claims.source: In comparison, merozoite invasion was significantly reduced in the presence of anti-CD55 antibody. Out of 312 merozoites that made contact with an RBC in the presence of anti-CD55, only 21 successfully invaded (6.7%) (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The number of invasion events per schizont rupture was reduced by half in the presence of anti-CD55 compared to control antibody.
claims.source: The number of invasion events per schizont rupture was also reduced by half in the presence of anti-CD55 compared to control antibody (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The efficiency with which egressed merozoites contacted an RBC was similar in the presence of anti-CD55 versus control antibody.
claims.source: In contrast, the efficiency with which egressed merozoites contacted an RBC was similar in the presence of anti-CD55 versus control antibody (>0.5 s; Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Anti-CD55 antibody inhibits entry but does not prevent initial contact between the merozoite and RBC.
claims.source: Together, these results indicate that anti-CD55 antibody inhibits entry but does not prevent initial contact between the merozoite and RBC.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that merozoite-RBC contact efficiency was similar in the presence of anti-CD55 versus control antibody, but invasion was reduced.

claims.claim: There was no difference in the length of the pre-invasion time, internalization time, or time to echinocytosis in the presence of anti-CD55 antibody compared isotype control for merozoites that ultimately invaded successfully.
claims.source: For the subset of merozoites that ultimately invaded successfully, there was no difference in the length of the pre-invasion time, internalization time, or time to echinocytosis in the presence of anti-CD55 antibody compared isotype control (Figure 3E–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E–G.

claims.claim: Blocking CD55 does not impact pre-invasion kinetics, at least not for the merozoites that manage to invade in the presence of antibody.
claims.source: These results indicate that blocking CD55 does not impact pre-invasion kinetics, at least not for the merozoites that manage to invade in the presence of antibody.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that pre-invasion time was similar in the presence of anti-CD55 versus control antibody.

claims.claim: Approximately 67% of merozoites deformed the RBC in the presence of anti-CD55 antibody, compared to ~60% deformation efficiency with the isotype control.
claims.source: There was a small but significant increase in the efficiency of merozoite-induced deformation in the presence of anti-CD55 antibody compared to the isotype control: approximately 67% of merozoites deformed the RBC in the presence of anti-CD55 antibody, compared to ~60% deformation efficiency with the isotype control (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in the duration of the deformation period in the presence of anti-CD55 antibody versus isotype control.
claims.source: There was no significant difference in the duration of the deformation period in the presence of the two different antibodies (Figure 4B), suggesting that CD55 does not inhibit nor prolong merozoite-induced deformation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: CD55 does not inhibit nor prolong merozoite-induced deformation.
claims.source: There was no significant difference in the duration of the deformation period in the presence of the two different antibodies (Figure 4B), suggesting that CD55 does not inhibit nor prolong merozoite-induced deformation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that deformation duration was similar in the presence of anti-CD55 versus control antibody.

claims.claim: Almost all merozoites that invaded successfully induced strong deformation (scores of 2 or 3), regardless of which antibody was present.
claims.source: Almost all merozoites that invaded successfully induced strong deformation (scores of 2 or 3), regardless of which antibody was present (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Merozoites that failed to invade had lower deformation scores, the majority having scores of 0 or 1.
claims.source: In comparison, merozoites that failed to invade had lower deformation scores, the majority having scores of 0 or 1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from the deformation scoring experiments.

claims.claim: Blocking CD55 with antibody does not substantially influence the efficiency, duration, or strength of merozoite-induced RBC deformation.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that blocking CD55 with antibody does not substantially influence the efficiency, duration, or strength of merozoite-induced RBC deformation, and instead suggest that CD55 exerts its effect on invasion at a downstream step.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that deformation parameters were similar in the presence of anti-CD55 versus control antibody.

claims.claim: CD55 exerts its effect on invasion at a downstream step after RBC deformation.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that blocking CD55 with antibody does not substantially influence the efficiency, duration, or strength of merozoite-induced RBC deformation, and instead suggest that CD55 exerts its effect on invasion at a downstream step.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that deformation was not affected by anti-CD55 antibody, but invasion was inhibited.

claims.claim: ~80% reduction in the efficiency of P. falciparum invasion into CD55-null RBCs was observed as compared to control RBCs after ~18 hr.
claims.source: In traditional invasion assays, we observed ~80% reduction in the efficiency of P. falciparum invasion into CD55-null RBCs as compared to control RBCs after ~18 hr, as has been shown previously (Egan et al., 2015; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citation to Egan et al., 2015.

claims.claim: No successful invasion events were observed into the CD55-null RBCs, out of 310 merozoites that made contact.
claims.source: When imaging invasion in real time, we did not observe any successful invasion events into the CD55-null RBCs, out of 310 merozoites that made contact (Figure 5A and Videos 6–7).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and Videos 6–7.

claims.claim: There were 25 successful invasion events into the control RBCs, out of 197 merozoites that made contact (~11%).
claims.source: In comparison, there were 25 successful invasion events into the control RBCs, out of 197 merozoites that made contact (~11%).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from the live cell imaging experiments.

claims.claim: There was no difference in the number of merozoites per egress that contacted an RBC between CD55-null and control RBCs.
claims.source: Although invasion into the CD55-null cells was clearly impaired, there was no difference in the number of merozoites per egress that contacted an RBC (>0.5 s; Figure 5B) nor in the efficiency of merozoite-induced RBC deformation between the two genetic backgrounds (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: There was no difference in the efficiency of merozoite-induced RBC deformation between CD55-null and control RBCs.
claims.source: Although invasion into the CD55-null cells was clearly impaired, there was no difference in the number of merozoites per egress that contacted an RBC (>0.5 s; Figure 5B) nor in the efficiency of merozoite-induced RBC deformation between the two genetic backgrounds (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in the distribution of deformation scores between CD55 null and control RBCs for merozoites that did not invade.
claims.source: Moreover, we observed no significant difference in the distribution of deformation scores between CD55 null and control RBCs for merozoites that did not invade (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: CD55 influences invasion by acting after the period of erythrocyte deformation.
claims.source: These results are consistent with the findings from the antibody inhibition experiments, and suggest that CD55 influences invasion by acting after the period of erythrocyte deformation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that deformation was not affected in CD55-null cells, but invasion was inhibited.

claims.claim: ~60% of merozoites that attached to an RBC triggered echinocytosis in the presence of the isotype control antibody in cyt-D treated cells.
claims.source: Upon treatment with cyt-D,~60% of merozoites that attached to an RBC triggered echinocytosis in the presence of the isotype control antibody, and a similar rate of echinocytosis was observed in the presence of anti-CD55 antibody (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: A similar rate of echinocytosis was observed in the presence of anti-CD55 antibody compared to isotype control in cyt-D treated cells.
claims.source: Upon treatment with cyt-D,~60% of merozoites that attached to an RBC triggered echinocytosis in the presence of the isotype control antibody, and a similar rate of echinocytosis was observed in the presence of anti-CD55 antibody (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Blocking CD55 does not significantly impact rhoptry discharge or echinocytosis.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that blocking CD55 does not significantly impact rhoptry discharge or echinocytosis, standing in distinct contrast to what has been observed for basigin and Rh5, where blocking their interaction with antibodies prevents echinocytosis (Weiss et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that echinocytosis rates were similar in the presence of anti-CD55 versus control antibody.

claims.claim: Attached merozoites can induce echinocytosis in the absence of CD55.
claims.source: The results confirmed that attached merozoites can induce echinocytosis in the absence of CD55, providing additional evidence that CD55 likely acts downstream of rhoptry discharge (Figure 6D and Videos 9–10).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D and Videos 9–10.

claims.claim: The overall frequency of echinocytosis was lower in the CD55-null cells compared to WT (17% versus 33%).
claims.source: While the efficiency of merozoite-induced echinocytosis stemming from an individual egress event was highly variable in both genetic backgrounds, the overall frequency of echinocytosis was lower in the CD55-null cells compared to WT (17% versus 33%), attributable to several egress events for which echinocytosis was not observed.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from the echinocytosis experiments.

claims.claim: RAP1 localizes to the rhoptry bulb as punctate staining in merozoites prior to rhoptry secretion.
claims.source: Prior studies of RAP1 have demonstrated that it localizes to the rhoptry bulb as punctate staining in merozoites prior to rhoptry secretion, but after rhoptry secretion it can be detected on the merozoite surface or in/on an attached RBC (Howard et al., 1984; Richard et al., 2009; Riglar et al., 2011; Schofield et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: After rhoptry secretion, RAP1 can be detected on the merozoite surface or in/on an attached RBC.
claims.source: Prior studies of RAP1 have demonstrated that it localizes to the rhoptry bulb as punctate staining in merozoites prior to rhoptry secretion, but after rhoptry secretion it can be detected on the merozoite surface or in/on an attached RBC (Howard et al., 1984; Richard et al., 2009; Riglar et al., 2011; Schofield et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: RAP1 staining was observed in a donut or C-shape for merozoites attached to both the WT and CD55-null cells, indicating that rhoptry discharge had occurred.
claims.source: When free merozoites were allowed to attach to RBCs in the presence of cyt-D, we observed RAP1 staining in a donut or C-shape for merozoites attached to both the WT and CD55-null cells, indicating that rhoptry discharge had occurred (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: CD55 acts downstream of the interaction between RH5 and basigin, facilitating a step of invasion that occurs after release of the rhoptry organelles.
claims.source: Together, these findings demonstrate that CD55 acts downstream of the interaction between RH5 and basigin, facilitating a step of invasion that occurs after release of the rhoptry organelles.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that rhoptry discharge and echinocytosis occur in the absence of CD55.

claims.claim: A ~ 50% reduction in the number of merozoites attached to CD55-null erythrocytes was observed as compared to WT cells 90 min after addition of late-stage schizonts.
claims.source: Using a flow cytometry-based attachment assay, we observed a ~ 50% reduction in the number of merozoites attached to CD55-null erythrocytes as compared to WT cells 90 min after addition of late-stage schizonts, as has been observed previously (Figure 7A; Egan et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A and citation to Egan et al., 2015.

claims.claim: PfAMA1 and PfRON4 were frequently co-localized at the cellular interface for merozoites attached to WT control cells (~85%).
claims.source: Using confocal microscopy, we found that PfAMA1 and PfRON4 were frequently co-localized at the cellular interface for merozoites attached to WT control cells (~85%) (Figure 7B–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B–C.

claims.claim: For merozoites attached to CD55-null erythrocytes, PfAMA1 and PfRON4 were co-localized at the cellular interface in only ~40% of cases.
claims.source: In comparison, for merozoites attached to CD55-null erythrocytes, PfAMA1 and PfRON4 were co-localized at the cellular interface in only ~40% of cases (Figure 7B–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B–C.

claims.claim: Approximately half of the WT control cells with PfAMA1 and PfRON4 colocalized at the interface had an indentation at the point of merozoite contact, suggesting the merozoites were mid-invasion.
claims.source: For those merozoites in which PfAMA1 and PfRON4 were colocalized at the interface, we observed that approximately half of the WT control cells had an indentation at the point of merozoite contact, suggesting the merozoites were mid-invasion, whereas this was never observed for the CD55-null cells (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Indentation at the point of merozoite contact was never observed for the CD55-null cells with PfAMA1 and PfRON4 colocalized at the interface.
claims.source: For those merozoites in which PfAMA1 and PfRON4 were colocalized at the interface, we observed that approximately half of the WT control cells had an indentation at the point of merozoite contact, suggesting the merozoites were mid-invasion, whereas this was never observed for the CD55-null cells (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: CD55 is required for stability or progression of the moving junction, acting downstream of junction formation.
claims.source: Together, these results support a model where CD55 is required for stability or progression of the moving junction, acting downstream of junction formation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PfAMA1 and PfRON4 colocalization was reduced in CD55-null cells, and merozoites did not progress past early invasion.

claims.claim: In the presence of R1, almost no merozoites were detected attached to WT cells 90 min after adding late-stage schizonts.
claims.source: In the presence of R1, we detected almost no merozoites attached to WT cells 90 min after adding late-stage schizonts, whereas attachment to CD55-null cells was only reduced by ~40% at the same timepoint.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from the attachment assays.

claims.claim: Attachment to CD55-null cells was only reduced by ~40% at 90 min after adding late-stage schizonts.
claims.source: In the presence of R1, we detected almost no merozoites attached to WT cells 90 min after adding late-stage schizonts, whereas attachment to CD55-null cells was only reduced by ~40% at the same timepoint.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from the attachment assays.

claims.claim: CD55 acts after the moving junction is formed, and plays a role in its stability and/or progression.
claims.source: Together with the immunofluorescence results, these findings suggest that CD55 acts after the moving junction is formed, and instead plays a role in its stability and/or progression.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that attachment was only moderately reduced in CD55-null cells, unlike the complete inhibition seen with R1.

claims.claim: CD55 plays a critical role during P. falciparum invasion of mature erythrocytes, where it is specifically required for parasite internalization.
claims.source: We found that CD55 plays a critical role during P. falciparum invasion of mature erythrocytes, where it is specifically required for parasite internalization.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing that CD55 blockade or absence inhibits internalization but not earlier steps.

claims.claim: CD55 plays a unique role relative to other receptors required for invasion, as a host factor that acts after discharge of the parasite's rhoptry contents.
claims.source: As a host factor that acts after discharge of the parasite's rhoptry contents, CD55 plays a unique role relative to other receptors required for invasion, providing a crucial link between the ligand-receptor interactions important for adhesion and deformation and effective internalization.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing that CD55 acts after rhoptry discharge, unlike other known receptors.

claims.claim: Fully mature, CD55-null cRBCs can be generated efficiently from primary human HSPCs using CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing.
claims.source: In this study, we showed for the first time that fully mature, CD55-null cRBCs can be generated efficiently from primary human HSPCs using CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing successful generation of CD55-null cRBCs.

claims.claim: The reliance of P. falciparum on CD55 for invasion increased significantly as enucleated cRBCs matured into erythrocytes.
claims.source: We observed that the reliance of P. falciparum on CD55 for invasion increased significantly as enucleated cRBCs matured into erythrocytes, likely reflecting the substantial changes in protein abundance that occur during terminal maturation of human red cells, including for proteins known to act as receptors, such as basigin and CR1 (Gautier et al., 2016; Hu et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing increased invasion inhibition in mature CD71-negative cells, and is supported by citations about protein abundance changes.

claims.claim: Terminal red cell maturation modifies the requirement for CD55 during invasion.
claims.source: As clinical malaria is primarily a disease of mature, peripheral blood erythrocytes, our results showing that terminal red cell maturation modifies the requirement for CD55 during invasion highlights the potential drawbacks of using cell lines to study host factors for P. falciparum.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing different invasion phenotypes in cells at different maturation stages.

claims.claim: Anti-CD55 antibody blocked both sialic-acid-dependent and -independent invasion.
claims.source: In contrast to CR1, where antibodies are only inhibitory in the absence of red cell sialic acid (Spadafora et al., 2010), anti-CD55 antibody blocked both sialic-acid-dependent and -independent invasion.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing inhibition in both NM-treated and untreated cells, and is supported by citation to Spadafora et al., 2010.

claims.claim: CD55 acts distinctly from CR1 and the other alternative, strain-specific receptors.
claims.source: This finding is consistent with prior studies showing that the requirement for CD55 in P. falciparum invasion is strain-transcendent (Egan et al., 2015), and implies a model where CD55 acts distinctly from CR1 and the other alternative, strain-specific receptors.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that anti-CD55 antibody inhibits both sialic-acid-dependent and -independent invasion, and is supported by citation to Egan et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Merozoite internalization is inhibited in the presence of anti-CD55 antibody or with CD55-null erythrocytes.
claims.source: Our live microscopy experiments have added a new dimension to this model by revealing that merozoite internalization is inhibited in the presence of anti-CD55 antibody or with CD55-null erythrocytes, demonstrating for the first time that CD55 is specifically required for parasite entry.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data from live cell imaging experiments.

claims.claim: CD55 functions distinctly from the 'alternative' receptors required for apical reorientation and red cell deformation.
claims.source: These results suggest that CD55 functions distinctly from the 'alternative' receptors required for apical reorientation and red cell deformation (e.g. glycophorins and CR1), as blocking interactions between these receptors and their ligands strongly inhibits merozoite-induced deformability (Weiss et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that CD55 blockade did not affect deformation, unlike blockade of glycophorins and CR1, and is supported by citation to Weiss et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Echinocytosis is stimulated by changes in the red cell cytoplasm that occur once an irreversibly attached merozoite discharges its rhoptry contents into the erythrocyte.
claims.source: Echinocytosis is a phenomenon of transient red cell shrinkage that commences soon after merozoite internalization. Current evidence suggests that it is stimulated by changes in the red cell cytoplasm that occur once an irreversibly attached merozoite discharges its rhoptry contents into the erythrocyte (Volz et al., 2016; Weiss et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Volz et al., 2016 and Weiss et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Echinocytosis is inhibited by antibodies that block the interaction between PfRH5 and basigin.
claims.source: Echinocytosis is inhibited by antibodies that block the interaction between PfRH5 and basigin, implying that this interaction is necessary for rhoptry discharge (Weiss et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Weiss et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Blocking antibodies against PfRH5 and basigin inhibit Ca2+ flux into the erythrocyte, possibly reflecting formation of a pore at the cellular interface.
claims.source: These blocking antibodies also inhibit Ca2+ flux into the erythrocyte, possibly reflecting formation of a pore at the cellular interface when PfRH5 and basigin interact (Volz et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Volz et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Blocking interactions between glycophorins and CR1 with ligands using genetics, enzyme treatments, or antibody blockade inhibits echinocytosis.
claims.source: The glycophorins and CR1 act early in the pre-invasion phase during apical reorientation, and blocking their interactions with ligands using genetics, enzyme treatments, or antibody blockade also inhibits echinocytosis (Volz et al., 2016; Weiss et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Volz et al., 2016 and Weiss et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Echinocytosis is not prevented by treatment with the actin polymerization inhibitor cyt-D or reagents that block the interaction of PfAMA1 and the RON complex.
claims.source: In contrast, echinocytosis is not prevented by treatment with the actin polymerization inhibitor cyt-D or reagents that block the interaction of PfAMA1 and the RON complex.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about echinocytosis.

claims.claim: The stimulus for echinocytosis occurs after the interaction of PfRH5 with basigin, but before establishment of the moving junction.
claims.source: Together, these findings demonstrate that the stimulus for echinocytosis occurs after the interaction of PfRH5 with basigin, but before establishment of the moving junction.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that echinocytosis is inhibited by blocking PfRH5-basigin but not by blocking PfAMA1-RON.

claims.claim: The current model of the moving junction involves interactions between PfAMA1 expressed on the merozoite surface and the PfRON complex inserted into the red cell membrane, independent of any host-encoded receptors.
claims.source: The current model of the moving junction involves interactions between PfAMA1 expressed on the merozoite surface and the PfRON complex inserted into the red cell membrane, independent of any host-encoded receptors (Alexander et al., 2006; Alexander et al., 2005; Besteiro et al., 2009; Richard et al., 2010; Riglar et al., 2011; Srinivasan et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: The moving junction has been proposed to be important for formation of the parasitophorous vacuole.
claims.source: In addition to its key role in internalization, the moving junction has also been proposed to be important for formation of the parasitophorous vacuole (PV) (Yap et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yap et al., 2014.

claims.claim: CD55 is required not for formation of the moving junction, but for its stability or progression.
claims.source: Consistent with this model, irreversible attachment of merozoites to RBCs was completely inhibited in the presence of the junction-blocking R1 peptide, but only moderately inhibited in the absence of CD55, suggesting that CD55 is required not for formation of the moving junction, but for its stability or progression.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that attachment was only moderately reduced in CD55-null cells, unlike the complete inhibition seen with R1.

claims.claim: Spreading of RAP1 across the RBC surface has been described for merozoites attached in the presence of R1, and has been speculated to reflect impaired sealing of the moving junction.
claims.source: Spreading of RAP1 across the RBC surface has been previously described for merozoites attached in the presence of the R1 peptide, and has been postulated to reflect insufficient sealing of the tight junction (Riglar et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Riglar et al., 2011.

claims.claim: CD55 or its interacting partners may hold potential as therapeutic targets for malaria.
claims.source: As the requirement for CD55 is strain-transcendent, these results suggest that CD55 or its interacting partners may hold potential as therapeutic targets for malaria.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation that CD55 is required for invasion across multiple strains.

results.result: CD55-null cultured red blood cells (cRBCs) were successfully generated from primary human HSPCs using CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing with ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes. A single sgRNA targeting exon 1 resulted in ~70% CD55-null cRBCs, while dual sgRNAs targeting exons 1 and 2 increased knockout efficiency to ~90%. The CD55-null cells proliferated ~10,000-fold with >90% enucleation rate, demonstrating that CD55 is not required for erythroid differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 and C89 are well-supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The CRISPR-Cas9 methodology is appropriately cited (Hendel et al., 2015), knockout efficiency is quantified by flow cytometry, and differentiation metrics (proliferation and enucleation) are documented. The conclusion that CD55 is not required for differentiation is appropriately inferred from equivalent differentiation in knockout and control cells.

results.result: CD55 is critical for P. falciparum invasion of fully mature erythrocytes, with the requirement for CD55 increasing significantly as cRBCs mature. Invasion into day 18 CD55-CRISPR cRBCs was reduced by ~40%, but when CD71-negative (mature) cRBCs were isolated, invasion was reduced by ~75%. Immunofluorescence confirmed that invasion was restricted to CD55-positive cells (22.5% parasitemia) versus CD55-null cells (<0.5% parasitemia). This demonstrates that terminal red cell maturation modifies the requirement for CD55 during invasion.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C38 and C90-C91 are strongly supported by experimental data in Figure 1C-G and Figure 1D. The maturation-dependent phenotype is well-documented with CD71 expression analysis and reticulocyte staining. The invasion restriction to CD55-positive cells provides compelling evidence. The hypothesis about maturation effects (C39, C90) is appropriately supported by citations about protein expression changes during reticulocyte maturation. Statistical significance is demonstrated with appropriate replicates.

results.result: Anti-CD55 antibodies inhibit P. falciparum invasion in a dose-dependent manner. Combined monoclonal antibodies (BRIC 230, BRIC 110, BRIC 216) and polyclonal anti-CD55 antibody both reduced parasitemia by ~40% at maximum concentrations. Importantly, anti-CD55 antibody blocked both sialic-acid-dependent and -independent invasion pathways, demonstrating that CD55 acts distinctly from CR1 and other strain-specific receptors. Monovalent Fab fragments recapitulated the inhibitory activity, confirming the effect is not due to antibody crosslinking.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C47 and C92-C93 are well-supported by experimental data in Figure 2A-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The dose-response relationships are clearly demonstrated, and the use of neuraminidase-treated cells provides strong evidence for CD55's role in both sialic-acid-dependent and -independent pathways. The Fab fragment experiment (C47) effectively controls for crosslinking artifacts. The comparison to CR1 is appropriately cited (Spadafora et al., 2010).

results.result: Live cell imaging revealed that anti-CD55 antibody specifically inhibits merozoite internalization without preventing initial contact. In the presence of isotype control, 15% of merozoites that contacted RBCs invaded successfully (53/345), compared to only 6.7% (21/312) with anti-CD55 antibody. The number of invasion events per schizont rupture was reduced by half, but the efficiency of merozoite-RBC contact was similar between conditions, demonstrating that CD55 is specifically required for parasite entry.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 and C94 are strongly supported by live cell imaging data in Figure 3A-D and Videos 1-2. The quantification of invasion efficiency, invasion events per egress, and contact efficiency provides clear evidence that CD55 blockade inhibits entry but not initial contact. Sample sizes are adequate (>300 merozoites per condition), and the statistical significance is appropriately assessed. This represents a novel finding demonstrating CD55's specific role in internalization.

results.result: For merozoites that successfully invaded in the presence of anti-CD55 antibody, there was no difference in pre-invasion time, internalization time, or time to echinocytosis compared to isotype control. This indicates that blocking CD55 does not impact pre-invasion kinetics for merozoites that manage to invade.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 are supported by data in Figure 3E-G showing no significant differences in invasion kinetics. However, this result should be interpreted cautiously as it only applies to the subset of merozoites that successfully invaded despite CD55 blockade, which may represent a biased population. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation in their interpretation.

results.result: Blocking CD55 with antibody does not substantially influence merozoite-induced RBC deformation. Deformation efficiency was slightly higher with anti-CD55 (67%) versus control (60%), but deformation duration was similar. Almost all successfully invading merozoites induced strong deformation (scores 2-3) regardless of antibody, while non-invading merozoites had lower scores. This demonstrates that CD55 exerts its effect on invasion at a downstream step after RBC deformation, functioning distinctly from receptors required for apical reorientation and deformation.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C61 and C95 are well-supported by data in Figure 4A-D. The deformation scoring system is appropriately applied, and the statistical analyses are sound. The conclusion that CD55 acts downstream of deformation is appropriately inferred from the observation that deformation is not impaired by CD55 blockade while invasion is inhibited. The comparison to glycophorins and CR1 is appropriately cited (Weiss et al., 2015).

results.result: Live cell imaging with natural CD55-null RBCs from an Inab donor confirmed that CD55 is essential for invasion. No successful invasion events were observed in CD55-null RBCs (0/310 merozoites), compared to ~11% invasion efficiency in control RBCs (25/197). However, merozoite-RBC contact efficiency and deformation efficiency were similar between CD55-null and control RBCs, confirming that CD55 influences invasion by acting after erythrocyte deformation.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C68 are strongly supported by live imaging data in Figure 5A-D and Videos 6-7, as well as traditional invasion assays in Figure 5—figure supplement 1. The use of natural CD55-null RBCs provides independent validation of the CRISPR results. The complete absence of invasion in CD55-null cells (0/310) is striking and well-documented. The findings are consistent with the antibody inhibition experiments, strengthening the overall conclusions.

results.result: CD55 acts downstream of rhoptry discharge. In cytochalasin-D treated cells, ~60% of attached merozoites triggered echinocytosis in both anti-CD55 and control conditions. Merozoites also induced echinocytosis in CD55-null RBCs (17% overall frequency vs 33% in WT). RAP1 immunofluorescence showed donut or C-shape staining in merozoites attached to both WT and CD55-null cells, indicating rhoptry discharge had occurred. This demonstrates that CD55 acts after release of rhoptry organelles, downstream of the PfRH5-basigin interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C77 and C96-C101 are well-supported by experimental data in Figure 6A-E and Videos 8-10. The echinocytosis assays with cytochalasin-D provide strong evidence that CD55 is not required for rhoptry discharge. The RAP1 immunofluorescence provides direct evidence of rhoptry secretion in CD55-null cells. The integration with prior knowledge about echinocytosis timing (C96-C101) is appropriately cited and logically sound. The lower overall echinocytosis frequency in CD55-null cells (C73) is noted but appropriately attributed to variability.

results.result: CD55 is required for stability or progression of the moving junction, acting downstream of junction formation. Merozoite attachment to CD55-null RBCs was reduced by ~50%, and PfAMA1/PfRON4 colocalization at the cellular interface occurred in only ~40% of attached merozoites (vs ~85% in WT). Among merozoites with colocalized AMA1/RON4, none in CD55-null cells showed indentation indicating mid-invasion, unlike ~50% in WT cells. In contrast, the R1 peptide (which blocks junction formation) completely prevented attachment, while CD55 absence only moderately reduced it, suggesting CD55 acts after junction formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C86 and C102-C105 are supported by data in Figure 7A-E. The immunofluorescence analysis of AMA1/RON4 colocalization provides strong evidence for CD55's role in moving junction stability/progression. The comparison with R1 peptide is particularly informative, showing distinct phenotypes that support the proposed mechanism. However, the interpretation requires some caution as the reduced colocalization could reflect either impaired junction formation or rapid junction disassembly. The observation of RAP1 spreading in CD55-null cells (mentioned in C105) is noted but based on rare instances.

results.result: CD55 plays a critical and unique role during P. falciparum invasion of mature erythrocytes, specifically required for parasite internalization. As a host factor that acts after discharge of the parasite's rhoptry contents, CD55 plays a unique role relative to other receptors required for invasion, providing a crucial link between ligand-receptor interactions important for adhesion/deformation and effective internalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 represent appropriate summary conclusions based on the collective experimental evidence from multiple approaches (CRISPR knockout, antibody inhibition, live imaging, immunofluorescence). The characterization of CD55's unique role is well-justified by demonstrating it acts after rhoptry discharge but before/during moving junction progression, which is distinct from all other known invasion receptors. The integration of findings across different experimental systems strengthens these conclusions.

results.result: High levels of other receptors important for invasion, such as basigin, may explain the reduced requirement for CD55 for P. falciparum invasion of younger, CD71-positive reticulocytes.
results.evaluation: Claim C39 is explicitly stated as a hypothesis by the authors and is based on prior observations about protein expression changes during reticulocyte maturation (appropriately cited to Chu et al., 2018 and Malleret et al., 2013). However, no direct experimental evidence is provided to test this hypothesis, such as measuring basigin levels in CD71+ vs CD71- cells or testing invasion in cells with manipulated basigin expression. This remains speculative and would require additional experiments to validate.

results.result: CD55 or its interacting partners may hold potential as therapeutic targets for malaria, given that the requirement for CD55 is strain-transcendent.
results.evaluation: Claim C106 is speculative and represents a future direction rather than a demonstrated result. While the strain-transcendent requirement for CD55 (C27) is supported by prior work (Egan et al., 2015), no therapeutic validation experiments are presented. The potential as a therapeutic target would require additional studies including identification of CD55's parasite interaction partners, assessment of whether CD55 blockade is feasible in vivo, and evaluation of potential side effects from disrupting CD55's normal complement regulatory function.

results.result: Background information on malaria epidemiology, P. falciparum invasion biology, and prior identification of CD55 as a host factor. This includes the three-phase invasion model (pre-invasion, active invasion, echinocytosis), key ligand-receptor interactions (EBAs/Rhs with glycophorins/CR1, PfRH5 with basigin, PfAMA1 with RON complex), and previous findings that CD55-knockdown and CD55-null cells show reduced invasion in a strain-transcendent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C27 represent established background knowledge appropriately cited from the literature. These claims provide necessary context for the current study but do not represent new findings. The citations appear appropriate and the descriptions of invasion biology are consistent with the current understanding in the field. The prior identification of CD55 (C21, C25-C27) is appropriately attributed to Egan et al., 2015.
